channel.title: Lectio Terra — The Earthly Book of Hours
channel.description: Weekly species studies, with readings and images, from The Earthly Book of Hours.

item.title: Lectio Terra: Shagbark Hickory
item.dc:creator: Ryan Weberling
item.description:
Carl Sandburg, Vladimir Nabokov, Charles S. Sargent

Few trees in New England, except perhaps the marvelous paper birch (Betula papyrifera), have quite the visual appeal of the shagbark hickory. The distinction is in the name. A fully shagged-out trunk embodies something between an elegant cascade and a strewn-out mess—a poise we might all hope to achieve, if we are so lucky.

item.description:

To untangle the messy world of squashes and melons, I will be spending the next three weeks zooming in on some of our favorite summer delectations, moving from the broad gourd family (Cucurbitaceae) to the distinctive melon-and-cucumber genus (Cucumis) and, finally, to the wholly separate watermelon species (Citrullus lanatus).

I came to appreciate butterfly weed through my wife Meghan’s occasional summer pickings. The plant’s clustered orange blooms can look like small flames or fireworks hovering above a meadow- or table-scape; or, if an especially long and narrow cluster is laying at rest on a table, it reminds me of a beaded brooch or hair clip.1 But I didn’t know the wonder or the strangeness behind the plant’s…

item.title: Lectio Terra: Corn
item.dc:creator: Ryan Weberling
item.description:
Haudenosaunee Storytellers, Emily Pauline Johnson

In my personal opinion, much resisted by the chatbots I consulted, corn is the berries of the vegetable world. Indeed, corn—specifically, sweet corn—is unique among commonly eaten plants in that it spans the typically distinct categories of fruit, vegetable, and grain. In other words, it’s a grass that produces sweet clusters that you eat like a carrot. The chatbots don’t know everything yet.

The lilac—so pure, so sweet, so artificial. Although only 20 to 25 species of lilacs exist in the wild, more than 2,000 named cultivars (according to the official International Lilac Registrar) have been developed, most over the past 150 years. item.description:

If there’s a plant that reminds me of God, it’s probably moss. Indeed, the plant’s biology is as ornate and rarefied as any systematic theology. Ubiquitous and abundant but amorphously changing, obvious but mysterious, perennially surprising and yet easy to take for granted, expanding or contracting as it slowly transforms its surroundings—modest moss can be as soft as the tender, mighty mullein…

item.description:

Paper birch (Betula papyrifera), also known as canoe birch or American white birch, is a mid-sized deciduous tree native to northern North America. It can be found across the northern half of the continent. Paper birch sap begins flowing near the end of sugar maple season, when daytime temperatures reach above 50 degrees Fahrenheit, and continues to run for only two to three weeks, approximately…

Welcome to maple time, if you live in my corner of North America. The sap of the sugar maple (Acer Saccharum) has been flowing now in most places for several weeks, and the sugar shacks are busy boiling off water to concentrate sugar. Sap runs vary each year in timing and length based primarily on temperature (freezing nights and warming days), though the sap’s sugar content is affected by…
